title: Turkey Rolls Out PKK Weapons Handover Mechanism as Thousands of Fighters Eye Iraqi Army Integration; US Displaces Russia as Ankara's Top Crude Supplier
subhead: Ankara's Kurdish disarmament process moved from declaration to implementation this week with a concrete weapons-handover mechanism and reports that thousands of fighters could join the Iraqi army under Turkish intelligence oversight, even as a resurfaced Davutoglu speech triggers a fresh insult probe. Meanwhile the energy map shifted sharply: Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries cut Turkey's Russian crude imports and pushed the US to the top of Ankara's supplier list.

sections.heading: Kurdish Peace Process Moves to Implementation: Weapons Handover Mechanism and Iraqi Army Integration
sections.body: Turkey's Kurdish peace process shifted from pledges to mechanics this week. Asharq Al-Awsat reports Ankara has unveiled a weapons handover mechanism ahead of the reintegration phase, part of the framework law Turkey's parliament adopted this summer to govern investigations, prosecutions and sentences for PKK-linked offenses. Kurdistan24 adds that thousands of PKK fighters could join the Iraqi army as the disarmament process takes shape 'under Turkish Intelligence (MIT) oversight,' while teleSUR notes Turkey is preparing the next phase of the group's disarmament. The process rests on jailed PKK leader Abdullah Öcalan's February 2025 call to lay down arms and dissolve the organization.
sections.whyItMatters: This is the first concrete sign of how Ankara intends to actually absorb thousands of armed PKK cadres, and the Iraqi army integration angle makes it a trilateral Turkish-Iraqi-Kurdish project rather than a purely internal one — the sensitive part is who vouches for the process and how Baghdad and Erbil accommodate it.

sections.heading: Tension Beneath the Process: Diyarbakir Detentions Over PKK Memorials
sections.body: The pace of reconciliation is colliding with its critics. The Diyarbakir bar of the Association of Lawyers for Freedom (ÖHD) says police detained 10 people in early-morning raids on Thursday for attending memorial gatherings for PKK members killed in clashes, including tents set up in Koyuyolu Park in the Baglar district. That park hosted an August memorial for 49 slain PKK members attended by DEM Party co-chair Tuncer Bakirhan. Turkish Minute reports the detentions drew criticism as incompatible with the 'spirit' of the process, after former AKP lawmaker Samil Tayyar argued such gatherings risked undermining state efforts to resolve the conflict.
sections.whyItMatters: It shows the peace track and the security-track reflex are running in parallel — exactly the kind of friction that has sunk previous attempts. How far Ankara lets memorial events and political organizing proceed will be the real test of whether this process is different from the 2013-15 round.

sections.heading: Domestic Politics: Former PM Davutoglu Probed Over Resurfaced Erdogan Insult Remarks
sections.body: The Ankara Chief Public Prosecutor's Office opened an investigation Thursday into former prime minister Ahmet Davutoglu on suspicion of insulting President Erdogan, according to Bloomberg and Turkish Minute. At issue are remarks from a September 2021 video, recorded during a visit to Bingol, that resurfaced on social media. In them Davutoglu said he lost the premiership for refusing to enrich himself, and appeared to reference Erdogan's son-in-law Berat Albayrak and 'five contractors' — the construction groups (Cengiz, Limak, Kalyon, Kolin, Makyol) long attacked by the opposition as the 'gang of five.' The probe is under Article 299 of the penal code, which carries one to four years for insulting the president. The resurfacing comes amid renewed controversy over the wealth of Davutoglu's successor Binali Yildirim, who journalist Timur Soykan says faces claims of roughly 480 million euros in assets.
sections.whyItMatters: The case fits a familiar pattern of post-hoc criminal exposure of former allies, but the timing matters: it lands weeks after a court reinstated Kemal Kilicdaroglu as CHP chairman, and as Erdogan leans into opposition-bashing ahead of the next election cycle. Davutoglu, a founder of the Gelecek party, becomes a test of how much rhetorical space the government tolerates from ex-insiders.

sections.heading: Energy: US Replaces Russia as Turkey's Top Crude Supplier as Bill Soars
sections.body: Turkey's energy import map has flipped. Turkive Today reports that Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries nearly cut off Turkey's Russian oil imports while the energy bill soared over 30 percent, and Middle East Eye says Ankara is replacing Russian crude and diesel with American supplies. The Cradle frames it as the US displacing Russia as Turkiye's top crude supplier, a shift Nordic Monitor attributes to Iran-war disruptions and refinery damage cascading through the region. In parallel, AzerNews says the Russian-built Akkuyu nuclear plant is nearing first electricity as Turkey prepares to load nuclear fuel — Putin told Erdogan at the SCO summit that Rosatom will launch Akkuyu's first reactor in 2026 as scheduled.
sections.whyItMatters: This quietly reshapes one of the strategic pillars of the Turkey-Russia relationship: energy dependency. If American crude is now Ankara's primary supply, Moscow loses its sharpest leverage over Turkish pricing and policy at the same moment Turkey is deepening nuclear and defense ties with Russia — a tension worth watching in the SCO framing Erdogan is pushing.

sections.heading: Economy: August Inflation Eases to 31.5% as Reserves Dip
sections.body: Turkey's annual inflation cooled slightly to 31.5 percent in August, according to RTE and ING, against a forecast of 31.62 percent and a prior 31.75 percent. Gulf Times notes monthly inflation came in at 1.84 percent, just below expectations, with ING flagging that fuel risks remain. The central bank has been normalizing funding while the market awaited the print, Turkive Today reported. Newsquawk data show gross foreign exchange reserves fell to $71.11 billion as of August 28, from $74.23 billion the prior week, a sharp drawdown against a backdrop of a global bond selloff and oil-price pressure.
sections.whyItMatters: The disinflation trend is real but fragile — the reserve drawdown and fuel-cost pressures are the weak spots. With oil prices elevated and the lira's hot-money dependence persistent, the August print keeps the central bank's easing path intact for now but leaves little room for error if energy costs feed through.

sections.heading: Aegean Flashpoint: Erdogan Revives 'Casus Belli' Threats After Greece-Israel Achilles Shield
sections.body: Greece-Israel's landmark defense pact continues to reverberate. After Athens and Tel Aviv sealed the multi-billion-euro Achilles Shield air-defense deal (roughly 3 billion euros, per Reuters and politico.eu), Greek and Israeli media report Erdogan has revived threats over the Aegean islands, with pro-government outlets describing Greece as a 'bad neighbor' and a 'pawn of Israel.' Greek PM Kyriakos Mitsotakis responded that Greece will take no instructions on its defense from anyone, drawing an EU red line around the Aegean and Greece's new defense doctrine, per Pagenews and Greek City Times. Israel Hayom casts the shield as a shift in the balance of power against Erdogan.
sections.whyItMatters: The Achilles Shield deal has hardened Greek deterrence and handed Athens a NATO-internal counterweight to Turkish naval pressure. Erdogan's rhetorical escalation over the islands is partly domestic positioning, but combined with Turkish research-ship activity and 'Blue Homeland' signaling it raises the risk of a low-level Aegean incident at a moment when NATO's southern flank is already strained.

bottomLine: The two defining developments of the day are implementation and reconfiguration. On the Kurdish file, Ankara has moved from Öcalan's disarmament call to a concrete weapons-handover mechanism — with thousands of fighters reportedly set to join the Iraqi army under Turkish intelligence oversight — making this the most operationally advanced phase of any Turkish peace effort in a decade, even as Diyarbakır detentions expose the limits of tolerance. In energy, US crude has displaced Russia as Turkey's top supplier under the weight of Ukrainian refinery strikes, chipping away at Moscow's oldest form of leverage over Ankara even as Erdogan courts deeper SCO and nuclear ties with Putin. Add a fresh criminal probe of former premier Davutoglu and an Aegean tempest reignited by the Greece-Israel Achilles Shield deal, and the picture is a Turkey that is moving on multiple fronts at once — toward Baghdad and the Kurds, away from Russian crude, and into a more volatile confrontation with Greece — with the Davutoglu case a reminder that domestic political consolidation remains firmly on the agenda.
